> **Follow Thy Fair Sun, Unhappy Shadow**

>
> ***

Pursue that beautiful light, sorrowful dark outline. Even if you are as pitch-black as the evening while she is constructed entirely from brilliance, you must nonetheless continue trailing your lovely sun. 

Track the person whose radiance strips away your own shine; for even though you exist in shame on earth while she is exalted in the heavens, you should still pursue the one whose brightness breathes life back into the world. 

Trail those untainted rays whose fierce beauty has scorched you so thoroughly that you are destined to remain dark until her compassionate glow transforms your pitch-black nature into luminosity. 

Keep following her while her brilliance continues to glow, because an unfortunate darkness will eventually arrive to extinguish her radiance—a tragic outcome foreseen by the miserable, dark figure.

outputs.L3:
In the grand tapestry of existence, few pairings are as starkly contrasted as the luminous sun and the mournful shadow. Yet, a solemn imperative drives this tragic dynamic: the unhappy, dark shadow must ceaselessly trail the radiant, sun-like figure. Though she moves in elevated, blinding splendor and he creeps upon the low ground, he is urged never to abandon her wake. He must remain her constant follower, despite the vast, insurmountable gulf that separates their status and fundamental natures. 

This devotion, however, is born of a profound paradox. It was the sun’s own intense, burning rays that scorched the shadow, defining his darkness and marking him with pain. Yet, rather than harboring bitterness, the shadow clings to a desperate, tender hope. He believes that the very source of his suffering might one day prove to be his redemption—that her fierce light will eventually soften into a compassionate grace, transforming his abyssal dark into a brilliance matching her own.

As they move through the world, their shared existence is defined by a bitter inequality. Wherever she steps, the sun is continually revered and celebrated, adored by all as a divine beacon of life and beauty. In tragic contrast, the shadow is viewed with disdain, disgraced as a mere stain upon her perfection. He suffers the world’s contempt in silence, remaining an unloved byproduct of the glory he so faithfully follows.

Yet, the shadow possesses a quiet, prophetic foresight that the admiring world lacks. He foresees an inevitable, tragic night on the horizon—a cosmic darkness that will eventually swallow the sun’s splendor and dim her glorious light. This impending doom instills a desperate urgency within him. He knows he must pursue her with unwavering resolve *now*, worshipping her beauty and offering his silent companionship while her light still shines.

In the end, their tragic dance is dictated by a destiny from which neither can escape. Bound together by fate, the radiant sun and the disgraced shadow are doomed to coexist in an unbreakable bond. When the final, overwhelming night at last arrives, it will claim them both without distinction; side by side, as they lived, they will ultimately fade away together into the same quiet oblivion.

**The Umbra’s Vow**

You tread the heavens crowned in blinding gold,  
A radiant orb above a fallen sphere,  
While at your feet, banished to the cold,  
I creep, a shade disgraced, yet ever near.  

Though cast in shame, stripped of my former grace,  
An iron geometry commands my soul:  
I cannot turn my silhouette’s embrace,  
Nor break the tether of your bright control.  

From dawn’s first rise I stretch across the earth,  
A desperate phantom reaching for your fires;  
At noon I wither, mocked for my low birth,  
A compressed speck beneath your harsh desires.  

You offer no mercy, only scorching disdain,  
Glancing never down upon the dark you cast;  
Yet in this agonizing, relentless pain,  
My solemn vow holds faithful to the last.  

For such is fate’s irrevocable decree:  
I am the darkness born of your own light.  
I cannot leave you, nor can you be free  
Of the quiet ghost that trails behind your sight.  

And when at last your blazing fires tire,  
When time consumes the brilliance of your sky,  
We shall descend into the selfsame pyre—  
For when the sun goes out, the shade must die.

### **Follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow**
*By Thomas Campion*

Follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow,
Though thou be black as night,
And she made all of light,
Yet follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow.

Follow her, whose light makes all shadows glide,
Whose beams the skies array,
And chase the clouds away,
Follow her, whose light makes all shadows glide.

Follow her, while yet thy light doth last,
Though she yield thee no grace,
Yet follow in her trace,
Follow her, while yet thy light doth last.

Follow her, that scorns thee though thou yearn her;
There is no beauty where
She doth not appear,
Follow her, that scorns thee though thou yearn her.

Follow her, and comfort take though that she shun thee;
For which thy torment grows,
The same shall end thy woes,
Follow her, her and comfort take though that she shun thee.

When her heavenly light is completely past,
Then thou shalt fade away,
And in her darkness stay,
Then thou shalt fade away, unhappy shadow.

---

### **Poetry Out Loud (POL) Notes**

#### **1. Poem Metadata & Eligibility Tags**
* **Line Count:** 24 lines (Qualifies for the **25 lines or fewer** requirement).
* **Time Period:** Renaissance / Early 17th Century (Qualifies for the **Pre-20th Century** requirement).
* **Original Context:** Published in Campion’s *A Booke of Ayres* (1601). Campion was both a poet and a composer; this text was originally written as a lute song.

---

#### **2. Key Themes & Imagery**
* **Unrequited Love & Devotion:** The speaker compares himself to a dark shadow hopelessly following a bright sun (the beloved), remaining devoted even when rejected.
* **Light vs. Darkness:** The central motif relies on stark contrasts—sunlight vs. shadow, bright grace vs. dark despair, life vs. non-existence.
* **Inevitability & Transience:** The shadow can only exist as long as the sun shines. When her light vanishes, the speaker/shadow fades away entirely.

---

#### **3. Recitation & Performance Advice (POL Criteria)**

* **Avoiding Monotony (Crucial for this poem):**
  * Because almost every stanza begins and ends with a variation of a refrain (*"Follow thy fair sun..."*, *"Follow her..."*), there is a risk of sounding repetitive or sing-songy. 
  * **Tip:** Shift your emotional tone slightly in each stanza as the poem progresses—move from helpless longing, to admiration, to painful acceptance, and finally to quiet resignation in the last stanza.

* **Voice & Articulation:**
  * Pay close attention to the archaic syntax and word choices (e.g., *"yearn her,"* *"yield thee no grace"*). Ensure every word is enunciated clearly so the modern listener can follow the logic.
  * Don't fall into an overly artificial "Renaissance accent" or sing the lines; speak them naturally while honoring the rhythm.

* **Pacing and Pauses:**
  * The second and third lines of each stanza are shorter than the framing lines. Use brief micro-pauses at line breaks to highlight the contrast between the short inner lines and the longer refrains.
  * Slow down for the final stanza (*"When her heavenly light is completely past..."*), allowing the quiet, fading conclusion of the poem to resonate.

* **Physical Presence & Dramatic Appropriateness:**
  * Maintain a steady, poised presence. The poem is introspective and somber rather than dramatic or aggressive; subtle vocal inflection will serve it much better than large gestures or theatrical movements.

### **Follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow**
**By Thomas Campion (1567–1620)**

Follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow!
Though thou be black as night,
And she made all of light,
Yet follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow!

Follow her whose light makes all things spotted!
Follow her that cures the blind,
The dead alive can bind,
Yet follow her whose light makes all things spotted!

Follow her, for she burns thy light attend thee!
Look how she burns thee quite!
And yet thou hast no light,
Yet follow her, for she burns thy light attend thee!

Follow her, alas, follow her, but old affection!
If she turn, look how she turns thee!
If she smile, look how she smiles thee!
If she burn, look how she burns thee!
Yet follow her, alas, follow her, but old affection!

Follow her, and if she turn, yet turn thee!
Follow her, and if she smile, yet smile thee!
Follow her, and if she burn, yet burn thee!
Follow her, and if she kill thee, yet die with her!

---

### **Poetry Out Loud Competition Details**
* **Category Eligibility:** Pre-20th Century (Written circa 1601); 25 lines or fewer (20 lines).

---

### **Recitation & Coaching Notes**

#### 1. **Musicality & Meter (Voice & Articulation)**
* **Context:** Thomas Campion was a composer and lutenist as well as a poet. This poem was originally written as a lute song (*A Booke of Ayres*, 1601). 
* **Coaching Tip:** The poem has an inherent lyrical rhythm, but students must avoid falling into a hypnotic, sing-song cadence. Focus on natural speech stresses while honoring the lyrical flow. 

#### 2. **Handling the Refrains (Evidence of Understanding)**
* **Context:** Each stanza opens and closes with a variation of the imperative line ("Follow...").
* **Coaching Tip:** Repeated lines run the risk of sounding flat if delivered identically each time. Advise the student to shift the emotional weight of each refrain:

  * *Stanza 2 Refrain:* Slightly more intense, emphasizing the paradox of her perfection making others seem flawed.
  * *Stanza 3 Refrain:* Urgent, reflecting the imagery of fire and consumption.
  * *Stanza 4 Refrain:* Melancholic and introspective.
  * *Stanza 5 Final Line:* Absolute, climaxing in ultimate devotion ("yet die with her").

#### 3. **Tone & Dramatic Appropriateness**
* **Context:** The speaker is caught in an unrequited, courtly love paradox—devoted to a beloved ("sun") who burns or rejects them ("shadow").
* **Coaching Tip:** Keep the dramatic appropriateness grounded. The tone should be quietly resolute, tragic, and intense—not overly whiny, theatrical, or melodramatic. The speaker’s strength comes from unyielding loyalty despite painful self-awareness.

#### 4. **Contrasts & Word Emphasis (Physical Presence & Articulation)**
* Highlight the stark binaries throughout the poem:
  * **Sun vs. Shadow**
  * **Black as night vs. Made all of light**
  * **Burns vs. Hast no light**

* Crisp articulation on monosyllabic verbs and sharp consonants (*black, light, spots, burn, kill*) will help ground the performance without requiring distracting body movements.
